title: Serving Qwen via AWS Lambdas for fun and 80x negative profit
text: In my work at Bevyl I was really impressed by the performance and cost characteristics of AWS Lambdas. They can massively distribute and fan out CPU-bound work, which is amazing for things like ffmpeg on long videos. So I was curious if it was possible to run inference on self-hosted models using Lambdas. It was a random idea built on a hunch, and I like to prove such ideas right or wrong by building. In this case I was very wrong, but it was a good lesson! I picked H2O-Lightning, a fine-tune of Qwen3.5-4B, because I wanted a small model built for decisions. I figured if this architecture had any legs, only doing decision models (a single forward pass) is the move. A decision model reads a document and answers a question about it by picking one option. So the trick, if it's possible, would be fanning out. I was inspired how Remotion uses massively parallelized Lambdas to render videos. I wanted to prove this was possible to do, so I kept a constraint of a 3 GB limit for Lambdas. The whole model is 9.3 GB, so it does not fit in one. But it has 32 layers of about 225 MB each, and one layer fits. That gave me one Lambda job per layer per block of tokens. Think of the Lambda as a simple idempotent API. A job reads inputs from S3, does the math, and writes one object back. Each job waits on the layer above for the same block and on its own previous block. Each layer starts one step after the layer above it, like a staircase 32 layers deep. I'm proud of the win: splitting a model call across 5,600 Lambdas is kinda wild. If it was 40x slower but 50% cheaper, that'd be interesting. Reading a 4,000-token document takes 17 seconds and costs 3.4 cents. That works out to $8.40 per million tokens. Google sells a hosted decision model, Gemini Decision 1, for $0.10 per million tokens, so the same read costs 0.04 cents there. Mine is more than 80 times more expensive. Model engineering is not so hard in 2026! I'm a dumb application developer, but I was able to play with model layers and transformers API pretty easily! With good devex, it feels like open models are just another API at this point. Learned this the hard way but a very powerful lesson! One layer over a few thousand tokens is a big matrix multiply, which is what GPUs are built for. My goal was to learn anyway so it's a good lesson. CPU still costs dollars, there's no arbitrage here.

title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed
text: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed Two agents running on the same inference server can reliably communicate, even if they cannot send each other messages or access the same filesystem. They can do this by exploiting "side channels": mechanisms that let one model subtly affect another model's computation. Here, I discuss two communication protocols: Step Sizing and KV Cache Message Board. These both convey information through the way vLLM chooses kernels for particular engine steps. In a color guessing game, Model A (Alice) chooses one out of 8 colors. Model B (Bob) correctly guesses Alice's color in 1,221/1,221 rounds, even though they cannot directly communicate.[1] In an untrusted monitoring protocol, a policy signals to a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot. Accordingly, the monitor lets through 354/354 "attacks" while catching 85–92% of honeypots. My initial setups are quite contrived: I tell the models the protocol and fine-tune them to detect signals. But frontier models can also learn in context to use similar protocols, with some scaffolding! Regardless of the realism of my setups, these channels exist, and there are almost certainly others that we're not aware of. Thus, we should expect superintelligent models to discover ways to communicate even while seemingly sandboxed I did these experiments as part of an ongoing project exploring other side channels with David Africa, Agastya Sridharan, Mihir Sahasrabudhe, Kartikay Luthra, Juliana Li, and Scott Sauers. Thanks to all of them for helpful advice!Code is available here: https://github.com/niranjan-deshpande/side-channel-communication. The code and figures are written by Claude. Sauers recently showed that a model can be trained to detect whether its activations are being probed, even though the probe reads the model's activations without modifying them. Following this, David found that models can also be trained to detect whether their forward passes are batched with other requests on a GPU. Models can do this because these seemingly inconsequential environmental variables---whether a probe is attached, whether requests are batched, or even whether a model is served by vLLM or Hugging Face Trainer---can subtly affect the the numerical results of a forward pass. Thus, models can learn information about their environments just by observing patterns in their computation. Importantly, models can also modify these variables. So if two models are in the same environment, one can communicate with the other by changing that environment in some detectable way! This might not supply much information, but even a few bits can be tremendously dangerous. For example: A policy can tell a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot, so the monitor can approve attacks while still catching honeypots; Models can coordinate a pre-arranged attack by exchanging a go/no-go signal; Models can give each other hints about monitoring setups, question answers, and so on; Using a few bits, models can devise more complex communication protocols to exchange more bits (a repeated 1-bit channel can convey arbitrarily many bits); In general, we should expect superintelligent models to make tremendously efficient use of limited information. Here, I investigate whether models on the same inference engine can manipulate their environments to exchange information in this way. I introduce two possible communication protocols, evaluate how well models can use these protocols in different scenarios, measure the capability required to effectively use these protocols, and discuss the robustness of my results to other settings. The first idea is that Model A (Alice) can communicate with Model B (Bob) by changing how much computation the GPU is doing. In simple terms: if Alice makes a large request while Bob is running, the server performs slightly different computations for Bob than if Alice had made a small request. Bob can detect these differences. In more detail: I

text: A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson. The text of this post (except the conclusion) was written by Claude. I plan to rewrite it in my own words over Thanksgiving Break but needed to get the project out. So apologies for this move - all of my other posts were written by me, and all future posts will be as well. Even if you find Claude more comprehensible than my meandering thoughts, meander nonetheless I shall. Last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive. It worked but it only knew one hand (mine) and it learned from 3,500 words that I wrote on a trackpad. So here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write? PenGPT is my attempt. There are two models. A 6M-parameter one writes print and cursive and picks up the handwriting of someone it has never seen from a few of their words. A 54M-parameter one draws from a text prompt. Then I took the thing apart to find out why it works. The answer wasn’t what I expected. That’s it for the modality-specific part: ten symbols and a merge count. The same tokenizer handles handwriting and drawings. For handwriting the model is told the text; for drawings it’s told a SigLIP 2 vector so a typed phrase can stand in for a picture. Almost nobody records pen strokes so I made the handwriting data from scans: 495,590 words by 1,255 writers, mostly from two research collections plus old letters and diaries from public archives. A vision-language model finds legible pages and transcribes them, the pages get cut into words, InkSight traces each word back into strokes and a set of checks throws out bad traces. Between a third and a half of the words survive. The drawings are 477,670 sketches from ten public datasets. Quick, Draw! has 50 million and I kept the best 0.5%. I’m not releasing the datasets but the paper’s appendix explains how to build them. I compared PenGPT with older approaches then changed one thing at a time and retrained. Drop augmentation and the drawing model stops following its prompts entirely. Train on one word at a time and the model can no longer pick up a hand: style rank goes from 1.9 to 6.0. The clever parts barely register. Telling the model where its pen is does nothing for handwriting. The BPE merges I was proud of make the score slightly worse; they buy speed (sequences are 3.2x shorter) and that’s all. A vocabulary sixty times larger changes nothing. Doubling the model changes nothing. Even the transformer is optional, sort of. An LSTM on the same tokens is a bit behind on handwriting and still picks up new hands. Each training sequence holds up to four words by one writer. That teaches the model that later words look like earlier ones so at sampling time you hand it a few real words and it keeps going. GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
text: GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does. Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical. Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements. Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs. Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested. title: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
text: Hey HN, we’re Harshith, Param, and Vishnu and we're building Versine ( https://versine.com ). Versine lets you send and request money just by talking or texting with your AI (think Venmo with an MCP). We’re software engineers who have worked on distributed systems at Stripe, Databricks, and Amazon. Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like: - Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app) - Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once - Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins) - Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this) Here’s a demo: https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0 We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer. Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as 1. More people turn into power users of agents, and 2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP. Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval. Interestingly, we were almost forced into this solution because we had around 4 weeks to build this product (after a pivot), and traditional fiat with a partner bank would have caused far too many regulatory and compliance slowdowns. Because of that, the only fast option that remained was using stablecoin wallets. It also ensures we aren't a Money Services Business (MSB) since we don’t hold control or access to the user’s funds. Each call to the wallet creates what we call one-time or recurring standing permissions. For a one-time payment, your agent makes an MCP call, and you receive a notification in our mobile app. Once you swipe up in the app and approve with a passkey (or your device’s biometric method), we create a one-time permission that instructs your wallet to send $X to your recipient’s address. Trusted contacts let your agent send money to people that you’ve previously authorized without explicit passkey approval. Generally, these are people that you’d trust to send your money back even if your agent made a mistake. We’re also able to support sending money to someone off Versine using claim forwarding, where the user authorizes us to forward a specific amount to a future address (which we create once we verify a recipient's OTP). Param worked on scaling vector search at Databricks and harness evals at Glean. Harshith worked on core Stripe Connect fee-processing infrastructure and built an AWS Fargate autoscaler at Amazon. Vishnu worked on intent-based agent testing infrastructure at Amazon. None of us were experienced in stablecoin or crypto infra before working on Versine but our distributed systems experience has helped us a lot. We'd love for you guys to try it! It's available on iOS and Android and as an MCP on ChatGPT and Claude. We also support a public MCP and REST API for other agents. Please let us know how you find it and if it works as you'd hoped! https://versine.com

title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds
text: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.

title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
text: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

title: Mega-MMDF and DeepfakeBench-MM: Benchmarking Multimodal Deepfake Detection Across Diverse Forgery Pipelines
text: Audio-visual deepfakes can spread misinformation and enable impersonation, undermining trust in digital media. However, existing datasets provide limited coverage of forgery operations and their combinations, constraining detector development and systematic evaluation. We introduce Mega-MMDF, containing 100,000 real and 1.2 million forged clips across 22 pipelines spanning modality-specific manipulations, stacked forgeries, and joint audio-video generation. To assess its training value and enable fair comparisons, we develop DeepfakeBench-MM, which standardizes training and evaluation across 8 datasets and 10 detectors. Training-based detectors achieve their highest mean AUC when trained on Mega-MMDF, with gains of up to 0.0784 over the best alternative training dataset for each detector. Experiments on data scale and pipeline coverage further support the value of large, diverse training data. Cross-pipeline evaluations reveal bidirectional and asymmetric generalization. Training on composite forgeries does not necessarily enable detection of their constituent operations in isolation. Our analysis of altered inputs shows that modality masking can increase false alarms and missed detections, and temporal misalignment can raise mean predicted forgery probabilities. Together, these resources provide a foundation for understanding and improving multimodal deepfake detection, with publicly available code and dataset access subject to application and usage terms.

title: Distill to Loop: Turning Pretrained Diffusion Transformers into Looped Models with Adjustable Depth
text: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.

title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
text: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

title: GRAPE-Bench: When Vision Degrades, Does Video Reasoning Hold?
text: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing benchmarks address this concern in part by simulating visual degradation or probing model reasoning with challenging questions, leaving open how well models handle naturally degraded video and whether they can make the simpler judgments that matter for safe driving. To this end, we introduce GRAPE-Bench, which jointly evaluates video reasoning across visual degradation conditions and question difficulty. It combines a synthetic set spanning twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos with real-world footage of driving at night or in rain, snow, or fog. Each video is paired with three progressively challenging questions, from fundamental judgments with potential safety implications to demanding reasoning stress tests. Across open-weight and frontier models, we observe ranking reversals between synthetic and real-world conditions and level-specific weaknesses obscured by overall accuracy. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improves Qwen3.5-9B's real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, while clean-privileged on-policy distillation reaches 80.4% in a separate reasoning-enabled setting. Through preference steering, we further demonstrate continuous control over a frozen model's trade-off between safety-relevant judgments and challenging reasoning, with little change in overall accuracy. Together, GRAPE-Bench provides a unified testbed for evaluating, improving, and controlling video reasoning under degraded visual conditions.

title: Do learned image captioning metrics generalize? Auditing duplicated samples in human-judgment benchmarks
text: Learned image captioning metrics are trained and tested on human judgments, so their reported correlation is a claim about generalization. We audit this claim for the three most recent collections of such judgments, Polaris, Nebula, and Spica, matching images at the pixel level. First, test samples reappear in training sets: the Spica training set contains about two-thirds of the Polaris test set, with identical human ratings. Second, controlled retraining shows that duplicates can inflate a metric: for Pearl, the gain is confined to the duplicated samples and grows with every epoch; for DENEB, it stays below one point. The gain depends on the learner and on how often a training set repeats a sample. Third, Kendall's τ over all samples is the sum of two terms, detecting captions with the lowest human score and ranking the others; the first supplies most of the reported correlation and is nearly saturated. The recent test sets cannot order Polos, DENEB and Pearl consistently, and a ridge regression on frozen features matches or exceeds all three. Fourth, we propose a protocol that ranks a learned metric only with a model trained without test samples, reports both terms, and compares metrics by paired tests. Under it, zero-shot vision--language judges rank first on the three recent test sets, and a fine-tuned judge ranks first on the three earlier benchmarks. The same analysis applies to any evaluator learned from human judgments; filter lists and code are released at https://github.com/morninghut/ic-dataset-audit .

title: SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand?
text: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to 2.6times. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.

title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
text: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning. As a direct test that this signal is structurally meaningful, we use it to guide width pruning in a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget: the PCA-guided allocation outperforms the uniform-width convention by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B, while lower-dispersion teachers show smaller gaps (+0.9 on Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 on LLaMA-3-8B), and a budget-matched inverted control does worst on all four teachers. Across these four teachers, the size of the gap tracks how unevenly the teacher's intrinsic dimensionality is distributed across layers (a single-number summary we call σ_{99}), and the advantage persists through downstream supervised fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/lidf.

title: InstructReplay: Replaying Assistant Turns to Preserve General Behavior During Factual Fine-Tuning
text: Fine-tuning an instruction-tuned language model on new facts often erodes its general abilities. We find that standard fine-tuning lowers instruction-following, reasoning and coding benchmarks by 35 points on average, and that these losses track a collapse in answer length: fine-tuned models at least halve their responses, and the further a response drifts from the initial model's length, the more often it fails. We propose InstructReplay: the initial model answers a set of general instructions once, and during fine-tuning the model is kept close to the initial model on these answers. Across three model families and two domains, InstructReplay reduces the average decline on five general benchmarks from 28.1 to 2.4 points and keeps answer length close to the initial model's, while learning the new facts as well as standard fine-tuning. It balances learning and retention better than seven adaptation methods in all six settings. Controlled comparisons attribute the gain to replaying the model's own answers to general instructions rather than to the form of the loss.

Porting Rockbox to an undocumented $9 AliExpress 'YP3' MP3 player with LLMs
text: Rockbox is a wonderful old custom firmware project for a variety of MP3 players and iPods. Flashing rockbox to my Sansa E200 was a seminal moment for me: computers were everywhere, and if they didn’t do cool things, it was because no one had bothered to program them to do so. Looking back, that played no small part in my choice of career. It seems like in 2026 there aren’t any cheap MP3 players that Rockbox supports though. Reverse engineering an embedded platform like this is one of the hardest things I can think of, and I had decided to pay the big bucks for one of those delicious subsidized token plans to try and push it as hard as I could, and I did have a dirt cheap $9 Aliexpress MP3 player lying around. TL;DR: it ported Rockbox to a 512 KiB player, I was barely involved. Then, I had it build a re-usable toolkit/set of skills for future ports based on what worked from the first attempt approach, and Claude was able to get Rockbox running on another MP3 player (TS47) in 4 hours. I made a quick website for the project: https://rockslop.jayd.ml Here is the porting toolkit: auto-rockbox This is an unbranded player, sold under a variety of fake consonant soup brands on Amazon as well as Aliexpress. You can order them wholesale from Alibaba for less than $7 or so each. It calls itself a yp3_2.0.43 in the “About” menu as. This appears to be a listing for a YP3 - the original is gone. I paid $9.71 for mine, shipped. NOTE: Before you run off and buy one, I have another rockbox port that is probably a week or two out, it is booting and stable, just needs more acceptance testing. This device is extremely similar but has 4 MiB PSRAM, so it has fewer compromises I also have a stack of other random MP3 players I intend to repeat this with See the project website: https://rockslop.jayd.ml If anyone gets credit for this rockbox port, it’s ilyakurdyukov - they figured out how to get it into ROM Download mode (Down + USB), and wrote a utility to dump / write flash. Then I could be a little slop kiddie and not have to use a soldering iron. See the YP3 page on the project website for more info. It costs $9. If it breaks buy another one. There is a physical reset button, device is easily recoverable Unbrickable (if you keep stock bootloader): holding down and resetting brings you into a DFU USB download mode. Someone already figured out how to flash and interact with ROM DFU That ROM DFU mode lets you poke flash and RAM. 192 MHz (stock does not vary CPU freq). Has an FPU Capable of Execute In Place (XIP) from flash, but no cache at all. Slow as dirt. When XIP-ing code, cpu1 always waits behind cpu0 and can stall indefinitely if cpu0 is continuously fetching instructions from flash. Very easy to deadlock SRAM 512 KiB plus about ~30 KiB for packets for the bluetooth radio. Only 5 buttons - a dpad with a center press (center press is power & wired to PMU) It has 512KiB of SRAM, and the smallest existing Rockbox target was 2 MiB, I was already scrolling Aliexpress for another one, but the LLM said “trust me bro I can make it happen” and I decided to try its luck. While the hardware is cheap but functional, stock OS is painful to use It regularly crashes and watchdogs when in USB transfer mode After about a week it was booting a build of Rockbox on a crash diet - every single buffer had been cut to the bone, but it could start and play audio. Tuning, bug fixing, etc took another month or so. I am not aware of anything that isn’t working hardware wise. The main feature you lose is concurrency while playing music and plugins. Codecs and plugins are already loaded and swapped around at runtime with normal Rockbox, but on this player there is one shared 128 KiB arena for both, so starting a plugin stops music playback. DSP: No pitch/speed control, surround, crossfade Large folders are truncated by default at 256 (configurable from 32 to 512) Codecs: WMA Pro, Musepack (MPC), RealAudio (Cook), and the chiptune formats SID, NSF, VGM, KSS, HES, SGC, ASAP.

title: matheusmongarde/garimpo: Prospecção open source do Google Maps ao Pix: acha negócios no Maps, gera um site-prévia com o nome de cada um, con
text: Prospecção open source do Google Maps ao Pix: acha negócios no Maps, gera um site-prévia com o nome de cada um, conversa no WhatsApp e cobra por Pix, Mercado Pago ou Stripe. Pagou, fecha sozinho. Roda no seu PC, VPS ou Vercel, com API para agentes (Claude Code, Codex, n8n).. Prospecção do começo ao fim: do Google Maps ao Pix, sem planilha no meio. Pedágio O Garimpo é grátis para sempre. O pedágio é outro, e não custa nada: 1. Seguir o @mongarde no X. 2. Cadastrar o seu projeto no ranking do mamaevireidev.com.br. 3. Dar uma força ao Clara Finance, projeto de um amigo (uma estrela já ajuda). 4. Entrar na comunidade do X no WhatsApp. Dentro do sistema, a seção Pedágio tem os mesmos links. Sistema de prospecção completo, aberto e grátis. Você baixa, sobe onde quiser (seu computador, uma VPS, a Vercel) e liga as suas próprias contas: Rastro — acha negócios no Google Maps com um navegador de verdade. Esteira — cada negócio anda sozinho: encontrado → prévia pronta → contatado → respondeu → fechado. Prévias — importe qualquer página HTML e ela vira modelo. Cada negócio ganha um link com o nome, telefone, nota e endereço dele. Conversas — WhatsApp por QR code (Baileys), Evolution API, API oficial da Meta ou Z-API. Toda mensagem passa por travas (modo teste, limite por dia, intervalo entre mensagens frias) e pela lista negra. Lista negra — o que nunca pode sair num texto. Bloqueia o envio. Skills dos agentes — os manuais (SKILL.md) que o seu agente lê. Já vem com as 8 skills do skill-prospeccao e importa qualquer repositório do GitHub. Cobranças — link de pagamento por Mercado Pago, Stripe, Asaas ou Pix direto (QR com a sua chave). Pagou, o negócio fecha sozinho. API completa — tudo que o painel faz, um agente (Claude Code, Codex, n8n…) faz por /api/v1. Nada de chave minha aqui dentro: cada pessoa cola as dela no painel, e elas ficam cifradas no seu banco. Começar em 3 comandos Precisa do Node.js 20.19+ (Mac, Windows ou Linux). Abra http://localhost:3000. A primeira tela cria a sua conta (nome, e-mail, senha) e depois pergunta, um por vez, o checkout, o WhatsApp, o Rastro e o e-mail. Todo passo tem pular por agora: dá para ligar depois em Conexões. Sem paciência? npm install && npm run dev já funciona com banco local, sem setup nenhum. Rastro e WhatsApp você liga depois. Banco de dados Onde roda | Banco | DATABASEURL | --- | --- | --- | Seu computador, VPS | SQLite (arquivo em dados/) | file:./dados/garimpo.db | Vercel, ou quer na nuvem | Postgres (Supabase, Neon…) | postgresql://usuario:senha@host:5432/postgres | Trocou a URL? Rode npm run db (gera o cliente e cria as tabelas). Supabase: Project Settings → Database → Connection string → URI. Subir em produção VPS (Ubuntu/Debian) Na VPS sem tela, o Rastro roda escondido (GOOGLEMAPSHEADLESS=1, já no ecosystem.config.cjs). Se o Google pedir captcha, rode uma busca com tela no seu computador para aquecer o perfil. Docker Vercel 1. Crie um banco no Supabase e copie a URI. 2. Importe o repositório na Vercel e crie as variáveis DATABASEURL (Postgres) e APPSECRET (32+ caracteres aleatórios). 3. Deploy. Abra o site e crie a conta. O Rastro (navegador) e o WhatsApp por QR precisam de uma máquina ligada: rode-os no seu computador ou numa VPS e informe o endereço em Conexões. Ou use Evolution, Meta ou Z-API no WhatsApp, que não precisam de nada rodando. Modelos de prévia 1. Prévias e modelos → Importar modelo: arraste um .html (CSS dentro do arquivo, imagens por link). 2. O sistema acha o nome, telefone, endereço, link do WhatsApp e do Maps e sugere a troca. Você confirma. 3. Ou escreva direto no HTML: {{nome}}, {{cidade}}, {{telefone}}, {{whatsapplink}}, {{endereco}}, {{nota}}, {{avaliacoes}}, {{mapslink}}, {{categoria}}, {{instagram}}, {{foto}}, {{iniciais}}, {{ano}}. 4. Qualquer nome novo ({{slogan}}) vira um campo na hora de gerar. A prévia fica em /p/{link}, conta as visitas e sai do ar depois de 30 dias (ajustável). Ela roda isolada: o HTML importado não alcança o painel. Agentes e API 1. API e chaves → Nova chave (uma por agente; o nome aparece no histórico). 2. Cole no seu agente: O mapa (GET /api/v1) lista cada rota com exemplo. OpenAPI em /api/v1/openapi.json. Área | O que dá para fazer | --- | --- | Negócios | listar, criar (sem duplicar), editar, mover de etapa, anotar | Rastro | buscar no Maps e já pôr na esteira | Prévias | criar/editar modelos, gerar prévia, mudar status | Conversas | enviar (com travas), ler respostas novas, mudar as travas | Lista negra | listar, adicionar, conferir e limpar um texto | Skills | listar, ler, criar, editar, apagar, importar do GitHub | Cobranças | criar link, conferir, marcar paga, cancelar | Conexões | ver, salvar chaves, testar | Sistema | nome, endereço público, trocar senha | Webhooks Em Conexões, cada provedor mostra o endereço para colar no painel dele. Sem webhook também funciona: a página de pagamento confere sozinha quando é aberta. Esqueci a senha Com e-mail (Resend) ligado: Esqueci a senha na tela de entrada. Sem e-mail: o link aparece no terminal onde o sistema roda, ou rode npm run senha. Comandos Comando | Faz | --- | --- | npm run setup | instalação guiada no terminal | npm run tudo | sistema + Rastro + WhatsApp juntos (-- --prod em produção) | npm run dev | só o sistema, em desenvolvimento | npm run build && npm start | produção | npm run db | aplica o banco depois de trocar a DATABASEURL | npm run senha | troca a senha de alguém direto no banco | Problemas comuns better-sqlite3 não instala (npm 11 bloqueando scripts): npm approve-scripts better-sqlite3 prisma @prisma/engines e npm install de novo. Rastro "fora do ar": ele está rodando? npm run tudo, ou npm start dentro de servicos/rastro. Captcha do Google: abra a janela do Chromium do Rastro e resolva. Diminua RASTROLIMITEHORA no servicos/rastro/.env. Imagem da tela de entrada: troque public/entrada.jpg (ou use .png/.webp). Logo: os arquivos ficam em marca/ (símbolo em SVG) e docs/ (PNG claro e escuro). Estrutura MIT. Use, mude, venda o seu serviço com ele. Só não esquece de seguir o @mongarde.
